c.tagline: The Beatles' waterfront city, where maritime grandeur meets football and nightlife.

taxi.fareNote: Licensed black Hackney cabs are metered and can be hailed on the street or picked up at ranks; private hire (including Uber and Bolt) must be pre-booked through an app and cannot be flagged down.

emergency.note: Dial 999 (or the EU-wide 112) for police, ambulance, or fire. Use 101 for non-emergency police and 111 for non-emergency NHS medical advice.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

avoid.reason: Late-night weekend rowdiness around Concert Square and Seel Street bars — usual big-city awareness.

hood_desc: The compact, walkable core around Liverpool ONE, Church Street, and Lime Street station, with the main shopping, the Cavern Club on Mathew Street, and easy access to Merseyrail; best for first-timers who want everything on their doorstep.

Liverpool's late-night engine room of converted warehouses around Concert Square, Seel Street, and Bold Street, packed with bars, clubs, independent restaurants, and street art; suits younger travelers and anyone chasing the city's nightlife and dining.

A former industrial dock district reborn as the city's coolest creative quarter, full of craft breweries, street-food markets, galleries, coffee roasters, and weekend markets; ideal for a hip, indie base a short walk south of the centre.

Liverpool's grandest residential quarter of leafy Georgian terraces along Hope Street, framed by both the Anglican and Metropolitan cathedrals, the Everyman Theatre, and the Philharmonic Hall; elegant, calm, and cultured.

The UNESCO-era waterfront around the Royal Albert Dock and Pier Head, home to the Three Graces, the Tate Liverpool, the Maritime and Beatles museums, and the Mersey Ferry terminal; scenic and iconic, right on the river.
lodging: Hampton by Hilton Liverpool City Centre

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink everywhere in the UK.

transit.pay: Tap a contactless bank card or phone on Merseyrail gates and most buses, or use a reloadable Metro/Walrus travelcard; ferry crossings are sold as individual tickets. A single city bus fare is capped at £2.
transit.hours: Merseyrail and buses run roughly 6am to midnight, with limited night buses on Fridays and Saturdays; the Mersey Ferry runs daytime commuter and river-explorer sailings.
transit.note: Merseyrail's electric third-rail network is the backbone, linking the underground city-centre loop with the suburbs and across the river to the Wirral; buses fill the gaps and the historic Mersey Ferry crosses to Seacombe and Birkenhead.

train: Merseyrail (Central, Moorfields, James Street, Lime Street underground)

car.idp: Not required for EU/EEA and US licenses

tip.r: Around 10-12.5% at sit-down restaurants if a service charge isn't already added; rounding up is common for taxis, and tipping is not expected in pubs or bars.

food.name: Scouse
food.desc: The lamb-or-beef stew that gave Liverpudlians their nickname: slow-cooked meat, potatoes, carrots and onion, served with pickled red cabbage and crusty bread.

places.name: Maggie May's
places.note: The city's best-known scouse cafe; a bowl with beetroot and bread is still under a tenner.

places.name: The Baltic Fleet
places.note: Dockside pub brewing its own ale downstairs and serving proper scouse upstairs.

places.name: The Philharmonic Dining Rooms
places.note: Grade I gin-palace pub with mosaic bar; hearty scouse and pies under stained glass.

food.name: Blind scouse
food.desc: The meat-free version, born of lean dock-worker weeks: the same potatoes, carrots, onions and thick gravy, still eaten with pickled cabbage on the side.

places.name: Maggie May's
places.note: Keeps a veggie pot alongside the meat one, exactly as Liverpool families always did.

places.name: The Quarter
places.note: Neighbourhood bistro that gives the classic a lighter, herby Mediterranean turn.

places.name: Ma Boyle's Alehouse
places.note: Long-running dock-side alehouse doing traditional Liverpool plates with good cask beer.

food.name: Wet nelly
food.desc: Liverpool's thrifty bread pudding: stale bread, dried fruit, sugar and spice pressed into a dense slab, warmed through and drowned in custard.

places.name: Cuthbert's Bakehouse
places.note: City-centre bakehouse whose wet nelly is the one locals send visitors to try.

places.name: Baltic Bakehouse
places.note: Award-winning sourdough bakery that bakes a rich, sticky wet nelly by the tray.

places.name: Maggie May's
places.note: Serves it hot with custard right after the scouse, the traditional order.

food.name: Salt and pepper chicken
food.desc: The house style of Europe's oldest Chinatown: chicken or ribs fried crisp then tossed with chilli, garlic, spring onion and five-spice salt.

places.name: Yuet Ben
places.note: Family-run Beijing-style restaurant trading on Upper Duke Street since 1968.

places.name: North Garden
places.note: Cantonese stalwart under the arch; trolley dim sum by day, salt-and-pepper plates by night.

places.name: Mei Mei
places.note: Roast-meat window and cheap, fast Cantonese cooking a minute from the Chinese Arch.

food.name: Everton mints
food.desc: Black-and-white striped boiled sweets with a chewy toffee centre, made near Everton's old toffee shop since the 1800s and still a Merseyside souvenir.

places.name: St John's Market
places.note: Sweet stalls sell them loose by the quarter alongside other old-school Liverpool confectionery.

places.name: Great Homer Street Market
places.note: Greaty's confectionery stalls are the traditional local place to buy a bag.

places.name: Everton FC club store
places.note: Stocks the mints that gave the Toffees their nickname; easy central pickup.

food.name: Meat and potato pie
food.desc: Northwest pub and bakery staple: shortcrust or hot-water pastry filled with peppery minced beef and potato, often eaten in a barm with gravy.

places.name: Sayers the Bakers
places.note: Liverpool bakery chain since 1912; the meat and potato pie is its signature.

places.name: Home Bake
places.note: Local bakery counter turning out hot pies and pasties from early morning.

places.name: The Ship & Mitre
places.note: Famous real-ale pub whose kitchen does proper pies with mushy peas and gravy.

food.name: Cask ale
food.desc: Liverpool is a cask-beer city, from mild and bitter poured in Victorian palaces to hoppy modern pints brewed in the Baltic Triangle.

places.name: Ye Cracke
places.note: Tiny back-street pub where John Lennon drank; a proper unhurried cask pint.

places.name: The Ship & Mitre
places.note: Dozens of cask and keg lines plus a long-running beer festival calendar.

places.name: Peter Kavanagh's
places.note: Wood-panelled, mural-covered snug bar beloved by locals for a quiet, well-kept beer.

food.name: Liverpool gin
food.desc: The city distills its own organic gin on Castle Street, and its cocktail bars have made it the base of Liverpool's late-night drinking scene.

places.name: Liverpool Gin Distillery
places.note: Working city-centre distillery with tours, tastings and a gin-focused bar.

places.name: Berry & Rye
places.note: Unmarked speakeasy with candlelight and expert classic cocktails; no sign on the door.

places.name: Some Place
places.note: Absinthe and spirits bar in a former shop, a Liverpool nightlife fixture.

landmarks: Royal Albert Dock
This magnificently restored 1846 dock complex, Britain's largest ensemble of Grade I warehouses, now brims with museums, galleries, and waterfront restaurants around a yacht-filled basin.
Pier Head and the Three Graces
The Royal Liver, Cunard, and Port of Liverpool buildings form the city's iconic Edwardian waterfront trio, watched over by the mythical Liver Birds.
The Cavern Club
The brick-vaulted Mathew Street cellar where The Beatles played nearly 300 times still hosts live rock and roll daily, a pilgrimage site for music fans worldwide.
Liverpool Cathedral
Britain's largest cathedral, Giles Gilbert Scott's colossal Gothic-revival masterpiece in red sandstone, offers tower-top panoramas and houses the UK's heaviest ringing bells.
Metropolitan Cathedral of Christ the King
Nicknamed 'Paddy's Wigwam,' this striking 1967 circular Catholic cathedral crowns Hope Street with a lantern tower of kaleidoscopic stained glass by John Piper.
St George's Hall
One of the world's finest neoclassical buildings, this 1854 colossus opposite Lime Street station dazzles with its Minton-tiled Great Hall and towering columns.
The Beatles Story
The world's largest permanent Beatles exhibition walks fans through the Fab Four's rise, from Hamburg dives to Abbey Road, with replica Cavern and Casbah sets.
Anfield Stadium
Liverpool FC's fabled home offers stadium tours through the players' tunnel beneath the 'This Is Anfield' sign, with the Kop's roar echoing on matchdays.
Walker Art Gallery
Dubbed 'the National Gallery of the North,' this grand Victorian museum holds outstanding Pre-Raphaelites, Rembrandts, and Rubens amid marble halls on William Brown Street.
Museum of Liverpool
In a bold white waterfront building at Pier Head, this free museum tells the city's story from docklands and diaspora to football and Merseybeat.

train.note: Liverpool Lime Street is the intercity terminus, with fast Avanti West Coast trains to London Euston (~2h10), TransPennine services to Manchester, Leeds, and Newcastle, and Northern regional trains; Merseyrail's electric network covers the city, suburbs, and the Wirral. No direct international rail.

bus.note: National Express and Megabus coaches link Liverpool ONE Bus Station with London, Manchester, Birmingham, and airports across the UK.

intl.to: Douglas, Isle of Man - from Liverpool ferry terminal
intl.op: Isle of Man Steam Packet Company

ferry.note: The Isle of Man Steam Packet Company sails from Liverpool's ferry terminal to Douglas; Stena Line runs Birkenhead-Belfast car ferries, and the historic Mersey Ferry makes river crossings and commuter runs to Seacombe and Woodside.

half.name: Chester
half.blurb: A Roman-founded city about 40 minutes from Liverpool by train, with intact medieval walls and covered two-tier shopping galleries called the Rows.

half.name: Southport
half.blurb: A seaside town roughly 40 minutes from Liverpool with a Victorian pier, a promenade, and the Pleasureland amusement park.

half.name: Manchester
half.blurb: England's third-largest city about 35 minutes from Liverpool by train, with a dense museum and gallery district around its rebuilt city center.

full.name: Lake District (Windermere)
full.blurb: England's largest national park about two hours from Liverpool, centered on Windermere lake with boat cruises and fell-walking trails nearby.
